shape, size and ndim.simple: Shape batata hai array ka dhancha — jaise 2 rows aur 3 columns. Size batata hai total kitne number hain, aur ndim batata hai kitne 'dabbe' (axes) hain: ek line ka ndim 1, table ka 2.
shape, size and ndim.pro: Shape is a tuple of axis lengths, size is their product, and ndim is the count of axes. Printing all three together is the fastest way to catch a transposed or flattened array before it reaches a model.

dtype and itemsize.simple: Dtype batata hai array me kaise number hain — pure integer ya decimal (float). Itemsize batata hai ek number kitni memory leta hai, jaise int64 ka 8 byte.
dtype and itemsize.pro: dtype fixes the element type and itemsize its width in bytes; nbytes is their product with size. Downcasting to a narrower dtype is a deliberate memory trade that must be checked against the value range.

Axis means the direction that is collaps.simple: Jis axis ka naam doge, wahi axis gayab ho jaata hai. axis=0 ka matlab rows ko mila do (columns bachenge), axis=1 ka matlab columns ko mila do.
Axis means the direction that is collaps.pro: The axis argument names the axis that is reduced away, not the one preserved. A (2, 3) reduction with axis=0 returns three values, one per column, and drops the row dimension.

len counts the first axis only.simple: len(array) sirf pehla axis ginta hai — table me rows. Saare numbers ginne hain to size use karo.
len counts the first axis only.pro: len calls the first axis length, so on a (3, 4) array it returns 3 while size returns 12. Use shape[0] and shape[1] when both counts matter, and never use len as a sample count.

Transpose swaps the shape.simple: Transpose rows ko columns bana deta hai. Shape (3, 4) ka transpose (4, 3) ho jaata hai, par numbers ka order wahi rehta hai.
Transpose swaps the shape.pro: Transpose swaps the axis order, so the shape reverses and the strides swap with it. It returns a view of the same buffer, which is why the operation is free until a consumer demands C-contiguous data.

Mixed literals promote to float.simple: Agar list me ek bhi decimal hai, poora array float ban jaata hai — integer bhi 1.0 ban jaata hai. Ek dtype hi hota hai poore array ka.
Mixed literals promote to float.pro: NumPy promotes all elements to a single common dtype, so one float literal converts the integers to float64. That promotion changes memory width and makes exact equality unreliable, so pass dtype deliberately when it matters.

A zero-dimensional array has no axes.simple: Ek single number ka array bhi array hota hai, par uska koi axis nahi hota (ndim 0, shape khaali). `.item()` se asli Python number milta hai.
A zero-dimensional array has no axes.pro: A 0-d array holds one value with ndim 0 and shape (); reductions over every axis return one. Use .item() when a plain Python scalar is required, because the object is still an ndarray.

Bytes are shape times itemsize.simple: Total memory = number of elements × ek element ka size. float32 se float64 karoge to memory dugni ho jaayegi.
Bytes are shape times itemsize.pro: nbytes equals size multiplied by itemsize, so dtype is the lever on memory: float32 halves a float64 matrix. Account for copies separately, since a copy doubles the live footprint.

ndim counts the axes.simple: Jitne brackets ke andar brackets, utne axes. 3D array me ndim 3 hota hai aur index bhi teen lagte hain.
ndim counts the axes.pro: ndim equals len(shape), and every axis needs its own index. In practice ndim identifies the convention you are holding — (batch, height, width) versus (batch, height, width, channels).

Ten zeros are one dimension.simple: `np.zeros(10)` me sirf 10 numbers hain, ek line. `(10, 1)` do axis hain — 10 rows aur 1 column, jo model ke liye column banta hai.
Ten zeros are one dimension.pro: Shape (10,) is one axis while (10, 1) is two; broadcasting treats them differently. A feature matrix needs the explicit column axis, otherwise the vector broadcasts across rows and silently produces the wrong result.

Shape is a tuple you can index.simple: Shape ek tuple hai, isliye shape[0] se rows aur shape[1] se columns nikal sakte ho — badi value hard-code karne ki zarurat nahi.
Shape is a tuple you can index.pro: shape is an immutable tuple, so indexing it gives axis lengths you can reuse in allocations and reshapes. That keeps code correct when the row count changes between runs.

A matrix of one row still has two axes.simple: `[[7, 8]]` me bahar ka bracket ek extra axis banata hai, isliye shape (1, 2) hota hai. Model ko aksar aisa hi batch chahiye.
A matrix of one row still has two axes.pro: Nesting a list adds an axis, so [[7, 8]] is (1, 2) while [7, 8] is (2,). A single-sample batch must keep that leading axis or the model receives a vector instead of a batch.

Every attribute of an ndarray.simple: Shape, ndim, size, dtype, itemsize, nbytes aur strides — ye saat cheezein array ke baare me sab kuch bata deti hain. Strides batate hain har axis me aage badhne par kitne byte chalo.
Every attribute of an ndarray.pro: strides are byte steps per axis, so shape plus strides fully describe how a view maps onto its buffer. A transposed view keeps the same buffer with swapped strides, which is why the copy only happens later.

np.empty is not filled with zeros.simple: `np.empty` sirf jagah banata hai, usme zero nahi daalta — jo memory me pehle se tha wahi dikhta hai. Isliye use karne se pehle har cell bharni padti hai.
np.empty is not filled with zeros.pro: empty allocates without initialisation, so the values are whatever the buffer held. It is a legitimate preallocation only when every element is written before it is read.
